name: Lanolin
lead: Lanolin is a yellow, waxy substance secreted by the sebaceous glands of wool-bearing animals, mainly sheep, and recovered from wool washing; it is often called wool fat, wool wax or wool grease although it is mainly sterol and wax esters rather than a true fat.[1][2] Purified lanolin is a widely used emollient in skin care, lip balms, baby products and nipple creams, and it resembles lipids of human skin.[1][2]

For appearance, lanolin is used to keep lips and dry skin looking smooth, soft and uncracked. It forms an occlusive, water-binding layer that slows moisture loss, which is why it sits in lip balms such as Carmex and in rich balms for hands, elbows, heels and chapped patches.[1][2] Fitness and outdoors communities also pass around lanolin-based nipple and hand salves for cracked, dry skin.[14][15]

Lanolin is also a relatively common contact allergen, and Wikipedia describes the question of how sensitizing it really is as historically contested.[1] Registered trials have compared lanolin with other topicals for sore nipples in breastfeeding women; Wikipedia states that evidence for a soothing effect is limited.[1][3][4]

angle.text: Lanolin is applied as a balm or in moisturisers to lips, hands and other dry areas. Its lipid composition resembles that of the skin's outer layer, and skin studies reported by Wikipedia show surface roughness falling about 35 percent an hour after application and about 50 percent after two hours, with effects lasting beyond eight hours.

paras: Crude lanolin makes up roughly 5 to 25 percent of the weight of freshly shorn wool; one Merino sheep yields on the order of 250 to 300 ml of recoverable wool grease. Wool is washed in hot water with scouring detergent, which strips dirt, suint (sweat salts) and grease, and centrifuge separators collect the grease, which is then refined to a waxy solid.[1] High-purity grades are about 97 percent long-chain esters, with an estimated several thousand to tens of thousands of ester types, and derivatives are made by hydrolysis, crystallisation, esterification, hydrogenation and related processes.[1]

Hydrolysis yields lanolin alcohols, rich in cholesterol and strong water-in-oil emulsifiers, and lanolin acids, around 40 percent of which are alpha-hydroxy acids.[1] Grokipedia gives an approximate breakdown of about 48 percent wax esters, 33 percent sterol esters and smaller shares of free sterols, fatty acids and hydrocarbons, a melting range of about 38 to 44 degrees C, and an ability to absorb up to 200 percent of its weight in water; composition varies with sheep breed, age, diet and climate.[2]

sections.h: How it works on skin and lips
paras: Moisturisers act by changing how fast water leaves the skin. Wikipedia describes occlusives as products that lay down a water-repelling layer that slows moisture loss, with ointments the most occlusive form, and humectants as ingredients that attract water and are usually paired with occlusives.[17] Lanolin is listed among common emollients, and its description as an occlusive that can also take up water places it between the two groups.[1][2][17]

Its sterol and wax esters resemble the lipids of the skin's outer layer; Wikipedia reports that both form liquid crystalline structures and multilamellar vesicles, and cites bioengineering measurements in which a 2 mg/cm2 application reduced skin roughness about 35 percent after an hour and 50 percent after two, with effects persisting beyond eight hours.[1] It also reports that moisturising effects remained detectable up to 72 hours after five days of daily application and that lanolin's barrier-repair properties are described as exceeding petrolatum and glycerol; Wikipedia notes many of these figures trace to a single 1999 book published by a skincare company.[1]

Lanolin has been used in skin products for well over a century: the alcohols obtained by hydrolysis, a rich source of cholesterol and a water-in-oil emulsifier, have been used in skin care for more than 100 years, and an 1886 article in the Buffalo Medical and Surgical Journal is among the early medical notes on the substance.[1] In lip care, Wikipedia traces lip balm to a physician, Charles Browne Fleet, who developed the product that became ChapStick in the 1880s and sold the rights to John Morton in 1912, and says Alfred Woelbing created Carmex in 1937; wartime lanolin scarcity slowed Carmex production in World War II.[16]

Regulatory and scientific attention centred on allergy. A study at New York University Hospital in the early 1950s reported about 1 percent of dermatology patients allergic to the lanolin then in use; one estimate holds that not comparing with the general population exaggerated its sensitising potential by thousands of times, and a 1976 European Cosmetics Directive labelling requirement was dropped in the early 1980s.[1] Pharmacopoeia pesticide limits followed in 1992 (US) and 2000 (Europe), and refined grades are now sold for sensitive uses.[1]

sections.h: Use in lip and skin care
paras: Lip balms are one of the main places people encounter lanolin. Wikipedia lists common lip-balm ingredients as beeswax or carnauba wax, camphor, cetyl alcohol, lanolin, paraffin and petrolatum, and says balms work by forming a protective, moisture-sealing layer on thin lip skin.[16] The same article reports that some physicians have suggested certain balms are habit-forming or irritating, which experts dispute, and that cold wind, lip licking and mouth breathing are alternative explanations for repeated dryness.[16]

Outside lip care, lanolin appears in hand creams, heel and elbow balms, baby skin protection and richer moisturisers, usually as one ingredient among several rather than alone.[1][2] Product-label material for a US petrolatum and lanolin ointment lists temporary relief of dry, chapped and fissured skin and lips among its uses.[13] In fitness and combat-sport communities, members describe using lanolin nipple or hand salves to keep dry, cracked hands from splitting, a use passed along as a practical tip.[14][15]

In skin care lanolin acts as a long-acting emollient. Wikipedia notes studies suggesting it outperforms petrolatum for very dry hands and superficial wound healing, and records roughness reductions of about 35 percent at one hour and 50 percent at two hours.[1] Lip products such as Carmex use it, although some people find it irritating to the lips.[1] Grokipedia describes it as valued for chapped lips and dry or irritated skin because it mimics the structure of skin lipids and supports barrier repair.[2]

Lanolin also appears in facial and lip products, baby skin protection, liniments and moustache wax.[1] A US over-the-counter petrolatum and lanolin ointment label lists temporary relief of dry, chapped and fissured skin and lips among its indications.[13]

Lanolin is used on sore nipples during breastfeeding, although health authorities recommend other methods first.[1] People who wear CPAP masks use it to reduce mask irritation, and anhydrous liquid lanolin has been trialled as artificial tears for dry eye.[1] Industrially it appears in rust-proofing, marine coatings, brass-instrument slide lubricants, shoe polish, leather and saddle care, and water-repellent wool treatments, and 7-dehydrocholesterol from lanolin is irradiated to make vitamin D3.[1]

Lanolin allergy is often mistaken for wool allergy, and patch testing is used to confirm it. Different grades may affect the same person differently, which makes pinpointing the cause difficult.[1] A 1950s New York University Hospital study found about 1 percent of dermatology patients allergic to the lanolin then in use, but Wikipedia reports that the lack of a healthy comparison group later was estimated to exaggerate its sensitizing potential greatly; a 1976 European labelling requirement was overturned in the early 1980s.[1]

Pharmacopoeia limits on pesticide residues were added in the US in 1992 (40 ppm total, and a 'Modified Lanolin' grade capped at 3 ppm for uses such as open wounds) and in Europe in 2000, and ultra-purified white, odourless grades are marketed as low-allergen.[1] Standardised patch-test series such as that of the North American Contact Dermatitis Group monitor lanolin-related allergens.[5] Product labels advise stopping use if irritation appears and avoiding application over deep, infected or puncture wounds.[13]

Registered and published trials of lanolin focus on breastfeeding care. One compares lanolin with breast milk for sore and damaged nipples (206 participants), another evaluates lanolin for nipple pain (186 participants), another compares two treatments for healing nipple wounds (100 participants), and another compares highly purified anhydrous lanolin with coconut oil for preventing subacute lactation mastitis (100 participants).[3][4][6][7]

A 2025 randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in Qom, Iran, enrolled 133 mother-infant pairs to test a lanolin, beeswax and olive oil cream for preventing nipple fissures and reported lower nipple pain scores in the cream group on days 3 and 7.[8] Further randomised trials have examined lanolin with prenatal health education for preventing nipple pain and trauma, and lanolin against human milk for painful and damaged nipples.[9][10]
An older double-blind vasectomy study used a white lanolin hand cream as the comparison for EMLA anaesthetic cream.[11] No trials of lanolin for cosmetic or appearance purposes were found.

Lanolin is a by-product of the wool industry, and vegan or plant-based alternatives are increasingly sought by people who avoid animal-derived ingredients.[2] Its reputation among lifters and fighters is practical: T Nation members describe borrowing a partner's breastfeeding lanolin cream for cracked, dry hands and report it working well.[14][15] Dermatology literature continues to review lanolin as both a useful emollient and an allergen.[12]

lore.intro: Lanolin turns up in fitness and outdoors forums mainly as a handy balm for cracked, dry skin, with occasional mentions of lanolin allergy.[14][15]

claims.claim: Breastfeeding lanolin cream fixes cracked, dry hands
claims.believers: T Nation posters describe using a partner's lanolin nipple salve on very dry, cracked hands and say it worked like a charm.[14][15]
claims.experts: Wikipedia cites studies suggesting lanolin outperforms petrolatum for very dry hands; no cosmetic trials of lanolin appear in registries.[1]

claims.claim: Lanolin lip balm leaves lips smoother
claims.believers: Users of lanolin-based lip products report softer lips.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes some people find lanolin-containing balms irritating to the lips, and lanolin is a recognised contact allergen.[1][5]

claims.claim: Lanolin allergy is rare because it is natural
claims.believers: Marketing of purified grades presents them as gentle and low-allergen.[1]
claims.experts: Patch-test series monitor lanolin allergens; purified grades reduce but are marketed rather than guaranteed to remove risk.[1][5]

claims.claim: Lanolin is the most effective occlusive for chapped lips
claims.believers: Fans of lanolin-heavy balms say a thick, sticky layer keeps lips from re-drying overnight and through cold weather.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports comparisons suggesting lanolin outperforms petrolatum for very dry hands and notes that trial evidence centres on nipple care, with no cosmetic trials registered.[1]

claims.claim: Balm use causes lips to become dependent on it
claims.believers: Some users say balms seem to make lips drier the more they are used.
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that experts dispute claims that lip balms are addictive and points to cold weather, lip licking and mouth breathing as other explanations.[16]

claims.claim: Wool-derived lanolin is a problem for people allergic to wool
claims.believers: Some people avoid lanolin products believing a wool allergy makes them unsafe.
claims.experts: Wikipedia says lanolin allergy is often mistaken for wool allergy and that patch testing can distinguish them.[1]

card.summary: A wool-derived emollient wax in lip balms and moisturizers, with allergy history and trials aimed mainly at sore nipples.
card.aka: Wool wax, wool fat, wool grease
card.note: A recognized contact allergen for some people; purified grades are sold as low-allergen.

quick.overview:
Lanolin is a waxy substance from sheep wool that is refined into an emollient for moisturizers, lip balms, baby care and nipple creams.

It is described as long-lasting at holding moisture, but registered trials focus on breastfeeding nipple care and none were found for cosmetic purposes.
quick.mechanism: Its sterol and wax esters resemble skin lipids; it forms an occlusive layer and can take up water, which is why it is described as an emollient.
quick.risks: It is a relatively common contact allergen, though Wikipedia says its sensitizing potential was historically overstated. Purified, low-pesticide grades are standardized in the US and European pharmacopoeias.
